name: Bengali

script.overview:
Bengali is written left to right in an **abugida**: each consonant letter already includes the vowel অ (*ô*), so ক alone reads *kô*. To write any other vowel after a consonant you add a **vowel sign** (কার *kar*): কা *ka*, কি *ki*, কু *ku*, কে *ke*, কো *ko*. Some signs go after the consonant (া ী), some before it (ি ে ৈ), some below (ু ূ ৃ), and two wrap around it (ো ৌ). Note that ি and ে are **written before** the consonant but **pronounced after** it. Full vowel letters (অ আ ই ...) are used only at the start of a word or after another vowel.

Most letters hang from a horizontal **headline** (মাত্রা *matra*). Write the letter first, then draw the headline across the whole word. A few letters (e.g. এ ঐ ও ঔ ঙ ঞ ৎ ং ঃ ঁ, and parts of others) have no headline or only a partial one.

To show a consonant with **no** vowel you can add the hasanta (্), but normally two consonants together are fused into a **conjunct** (যুক্তাক্ষর *juktakkhor*): ন + ত = ন্ত, ক + ষ = ক্ষ. Some conjuncts are simply the two letters squeezed together; others look quite different and must be learned. Special shapes include র-ফলা (a slash under a letter for r: প্র *pr*), রেফ (a small stroke above for a preceding r: র্ম *rm*) and য-ফলা (a hook after a letter that usually just **doubles** the consonant: বিদ্যা *bidda*).

Spelling is historical, so several letters now sound the same (শ ষ স; জ য; ন ণ; ই ঈ; উ ঊ). You must learn spellings word by word, but reading aloud is easy once you know which letters merge. Bengali also has its own digits (০–৯), used everywhere alongside Western numerals. The danda (।) ends a sentence instead of a full stop.

where: Bangladesh (national language) and the Indian states of West Bengal, Tripura and parts of Assam (Barak Valley); large diaspora in the UK, Middle East and North America
tagline: The sweet, musical language of Tagore, Satyajit Ray and 280 million speakers, with almost no gender and very regular verbs.
intro:
**Bengali** (বাংলা *baṅla*) is an Indo-Aryan language, a cousin of Hindi, Odia and Assamese, and the seventh most spoken language in the world. It is the national language of **Bangladesh** and an official language of **West Bengal** and **Tripura** in India. 21 February, International Mother Language Day, commemorates students killed in Dhaka in 1952 defending the right to speak Bengali.

Bengali is written in its own **Bengali–Assamese script**, an abugida closely related to Devanagari: every consonant carries a built-in vowel (here pronounced *ô*), other vowels are added as signs, and consonant clusters are fused into conjuncts. The letters hang from a headline (মাত্রা *matra*), just like Hindi.

Grammatically Bengali is learner-friendly: **no grammatical gender** at all, verbs agree only with person and politeness level (never with gender or number), and there is no ergative construction. Instead you will learn **classifiers** (টা *ṭa*, টি *ṭi*, গুলো *gulo*) that attach to nouns, and **three levels of 'you'**: respectful আপনি *apni*, familiar তুমি *tumi* and intimate তুই *tui*.

This course teaches the **standard colloquial language** (চলিত ভাষা *cholito bhasha*) used in education, media and conversation in both Kolkata and Dhaka. Where Bangladesh and West Bengal commonly differ (water is পানি *pani* in Bangladesh and জল *jôl* in West Bengal; greetings follow religious lines), the notes tell you both. The older, literary সাধু ভাষা (*shadhu bhasha*) is not taught.
romanizationNote: The romanization shows how words are **said**, not how they are spelled. The inherent vowel অ is written **ô** (like the o in British *hot* or the aw in *law*), but where it is actually pronounced as a closed o (before an i or u in the next syllable, e.g. করি *kori*, গরু *goru*) we write **o**; when it is silent at the end of a word it is simply dropped (মন *mon*, কাজ *kaj*). আ is plain **a** (there is no long/short contrast in Bengali, so no macrons are used: ই/ঈ are both **i**, উ/ঊ both **u**). The vowel এ has two pronunciations: **e** (as in *say*, without the glide) and **æ** (as in *cat*), e.g. এক *æk*, দেখা *dækha*, কেমন *kæmon*: always pronounce æ as the vowel in *cat*. Because শ, ষ and usually স all sound like English *sh*, we write **sh** for all three (সাত *shat*); স becomes **s** before dental consonants and in loanwords (রাস্তা *rasta*, স্কুল *skul*). জ and য both sound like English **j**; ণ and ন are both **n**; য় is **y** (or **w** after o/u-sounds, e.g. খাওয়া *khawa*). ট ড are retroflex **ṭ ḍ**, ড়/ঢ় are flaps **ṛ**, and a dot-free **t d** is always dental (tongue on the teeth). **ṃ** after a vowel means it is nasalised (চাঁদ *chaṃd*); ং is **ṅ** (as *ng* in *sing*). Conjuncts are written as they sound: double consonants are doubled (বিদ্যা *bidda*, পদ্ম *pôddo*), ক্ষ is *kkh* (*kh* at the start of a word) and জ্ঞ is *gg* (*g* at the start, with æ: জ্ঞান *gæn*). **ph** is a breathy p that many speakers say as an f; **bh** is never a v.

pronunciation.title: The inherent vowel: ô, o, or nothing
pronunciation.body:
Every Bengali consonant carries the vowel অ, and it is **not** the 'uh' of Hindi. It is a rounded **ô** like the vowel in British *hot* or American *law*: কলা *kôla* 'banana', ঘর *ghôr* 'room'. Round your lips slightly and drop your jaw.

Three rules tell you what actually happens to it. (1) **At the end of a word** it is usually silent: মন *mon*, কাজ *kaj*, ঘর *ghôr*; but it is kept after conjuncts and in many adjectives and verb forms (বড় *bôṛo*, ছোট *chhoṭo*, শান্ত *shanto*, করো *kôro*). (2) It becomes a **closed o** when the next syllable has i or u, or before a য-ফলা conjunct: করি *kori*, গরু *goru*, বই *boi*, সত্য *shotto*. (3) Otherwise, especially in the first syllable, it is open **ô**.

Don't confuse it with আ *a*: the difference between কল *kôl* (tap) and কাল *kal* (tomorrow / time) is exactly this vowel.
tips: Say 'law' and cut off the w: that is ô.
Don't say Hindi-style 'kamal'; Bengali কমল is kômol.
When you see an i or u sound coming next, close ô to o.
If unsure whether a final অ is pronounced, listen: adjectives usually keep it (bhalo, bôṛo, chhoṭo).

pairs.note: ô closes to o before i

pronunciation.title: The two sounds of এ: e and æ
pronunciation.body:
The letter এ / sign ে has two pronunciations. Usually it is a pure **e** (as in *say*, without the y-glide): দেশ *desh* 'country', মেয়ে *meye* 'girl'. But in many common words it is an open **æ**, the vowel of English *cat*: এক *æk* 'one', কেমন *kæmon* 'how', দেখা *dækha* 'to see', খেলা *khæla* 'game'.

The æ sound is also written with য-ফলা + া: ব্যাগ *bæg* 'bag', ব্যাংক *bæṅk* 'bank', হ্যাঁ *hæṃ* 'yes'.

A rough rule: এ in the first syllable becomes æ when the next syllable has a or ô (দেখা *dækha*), but stays e when the next syllable has i, u or e (দেখি *dekhi*, দেখে *dekhe*). This is **vowel harmony** and it makes verb forms shift: দেখা *dækha* / দেখি *dekhi*. There are many exceptions (কেনা *kena* 'to buy', দেনা *dena* 'debt'), so learn words with their sound.
tips: æ is the vowel in 'cat', 'bad', 'man'.
In this course æ is always written æ, so trust the romanization.
Practise the verb pairs: dækha/dekhi, khæla/kheli, phæla/pheli.

pronunciation.title: Aspiration: k vs kh, b vs bh
pronunciation.body:
Bengali distinguishes **unaspirated** consonants (no puff of air) from **aspirated** ones (with a strong puff): ক *k* vs খ *kh*, প *p* vs ফ *ph*, ত *t* vs থ *th*. English speakers aspirate automatically at the start of words ('pin' has a puff, 'spin' does not), so the hard part is saying ক, প, ত, ট, চ **without** any puff, like the p in *spin*.

Bengali also has **voiced aspirates** (ঘ gh, ঝ jh, ঢ ḍh, ধ dh, ভ bh): a voiced consonant followed by a breathy release, like the 'gh' in 'doghouse' or 'bh' in 'clubhouse' said quickly. ভ is never v and থ/ধ are never English 'th'.

The difference changes meanings: কাল *kal* 'tomorrow' vs খাল *khal* 'canal'.
tips: Hold a tissue in front of your mouth: it should move for খ, not for ক.
Practise 'spin, skin, still' and copy that unaspirated p, k, t.
For ভ, say 'club-house' faster and faster until it becomes one sound.
ফ is often said as English f, and that is fine.

pronunciation.title: Retroflex ট ড vs dental ত দ
pronunciation.body:
Bengali has two kinds of t and d. **Dental** ত থ দ ধ: put the tip of your tongue **against the back of your upper front teeth**, like Spanish or French t/d. **Retroflex** ট ঠ ড ঢ: curl the tongue tip **back** to touch the roof of the mouth just behind the gum ridge.

English t and d are made in between, on the gum ridge, so Bengali speakers hear English t/d as **retroflex**: that is why 'table' is টেবিল and 'doctor' is ডাক্তার. Your job is mainly to learn the soft, teeth-touching dental sounds and use them where the spelling shows ত/দ.

Romanization: dotted **ṭ ḍ** are retroflex; plain **t d** are always dental.
tips: For ত, press the tongue tip firmly against the back of your upper front teeth.
For ট, curl the tongue back as if starting an American r.
If a word sounds 'English' (ṭebil, ḍaktar), it uses retroflex.

pronunciation.title: The flaps ড় and ঢ় (ṛ)
pronunciation.body:
ড় (and the rare ঢ়) is a **retroflex flap**: curl your tongue tip back, then flick it forward so it strikes the roof of the mouth once on the way out. It sounds a bit like a mix of r and d. It never begins a word.

The flap contrasts with the ordinary tapped **র** r, and the difference matters: পড়া *pôṛa* 'to read' vs পরা *pôra* 'to wear'. In some Bangladeshi and East Bengal speech the two merge into r, but standard speech keeps them apart.
tips: Start with ড, then let the tongue slide forward without stopping: that's ড়.
Words like বড় (big), বাড়ি (house), গাড়ি (car) are very common: get them right early.
র is a quick tap with the tongue tip at the gum ridge, without curling back.

pronunciation.title: Nasal vowels (chandrabindu ঁ)
pronunciation.body:
The moon-and-dot ঁ (চন্দ্রবিন্দু *chôndrobindu*) over a letter means the vowel is **nasalised**: air flows through the nose and the mouth at the same time, like French *bon* or the vowel in a long 'uh-huh'. There is no n or m consonant after it.

Nasalisation changes meaning: কাঁদা *kaṃda* 'to cry' vs কাদা *kada* 'mud'. It is especially common in verbs and in respectful pronouns: তাঁর *taṃr* 'his/her (respectful)' vs তার *tar* 'his/her'. In the romanization a nasal vowel is marked with **ṃ** after it.
tips: Pinch your nose: a nasal vowel will sound blocked, an oral one won't.
Don't add an n or m: চাঁদ is chaṃd, not 'chand'.
Keep the nasal through the whole vowel, not just at the end.

pronunciation.title: Many letters, one sound: শ ষ স, জ য, ন ণ, ই ঈ, উ ঊ
pronunciation.body:
Bengali spelling preserves Sanskrit distinctions that have disappeared from speech. The good news: reading aloud is easier than it looks. The bad news: spelling must be memorised.

**শ ষ স** are all normally **sh**. স is a real **s** only before a dental (স্ত st, স্থ sth, স্ন sn), in clusters with র/ল (স্র, স্ল) and in many English loans (বাস *bas*). **জ and য** are both **j**. **ন and ণ** are both **n**. **ই/ঈ** are both **i**, and **উ/ঊ** both **u**. **ঋ** is **ri**. The khanda-ta ৎ is just t. The pairs below are true homophones: same sound, different meaning.
tips: When reading, just say sh for any of শ ষ স unless a dental consonant follows.
Learn spellings visually: সব 'all' and শব 'corpse' sound the same!
In Bangladesh many speakers say স as s more often, especially in careful speech.

pairs.note: ই and ঈ sound the same

b.en: a watch of the night (3 hours)

pairs.note: জ and য sound the same
ণ and ন sound the same

pronunciation.title: How conjuncts are really pronounced
pronunciation.body:
Several conjunct types are not pronounced letter by letter. **য-ফলা** (্য) after a consonant in the middle of a word **doubles** that consonant: বিদ্যা *bidda* 'learning', সত্য *shotto* 'truth', ধন্যবাদ *dhonnobad*. At the start of a word it does not double, and with া it gives **æ**: ব্যাগ *bæg*.

**ব-ফলা** (্ব) and **ম-ফলা** (্ম) after another consonant also usually just double it: বিশ্ব *bishsho* 'world', পদ্ম *pôddo* 'lotus', আত্মা *atta* 'soul'. (But ম্ব is a real mb: লম্বা *lômba*.)

**ক্ষ** is *kh* at the start (ক্ষমা *khôma*) and *kkh* in the middle (পরীক্ষা *porikkha*). **জ্ঞ** is *g* at the start, often colouring the next a to æ (জ্ঞান *gæn*), and *gg* in the middle (বিজ্ঞান *biggæn*). Finally, a **visarga** in the middle of a word doubles the next consonant: দুঃখ *dukkho*.
tips: A hook after the consonant (য-ফলা) = say it twice.
Don't say 'vishva' or 'padma': Bengali is bishsho and pôddo.
Hold double consonants slightly longer, like 'book-keeper'.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants
pronunciation.body:
Many Bengali words have **double (long) consonants**, written as a conjunct of the same letter (ত্ত, ন্ন, ল্ল, চ্ছ, ক্ক) or produced by য-ফলা. You must hold the consonant for longer, as in English 'book-case' or 'black-cat' where two k sounds meet. Shortening a double consonant can change the word or make it sound foreign.

Aspirated doubles are written with the plain + aspirated letter (চ্ছ *chchh*, দ্ধ *ddh*): hold the closure, then release with the puff.
tips: Pause briefly with the mouth closed before releasing a double consonant.
Clap the rhythm: পাত্তা is pat-ta, not pa-ta.

pronunciation.title: ph, bh, and the missing v, z and f
pronunciation.body:
Bengali has no native **v**, **z** or **f**. ভ is *bh* (breathy b), not v; ব is *b*. So English 'video' becomes ভিডিও *bhiḍio* (or ভিডিও with a light b), and 'university' becomes ইউনিভার্সিটি. জ covers English **z**: জিরো *jiro* 'zero'.

ফ is officially an aspirated *ph*, but in everyday speech, particularly in Bangladesh and among younger speakers, it is very often pronounced as **f**: ফোন *phon/fon* 'phone', ফুল *phul/ful* 'flower'. Both are correct; this course writes *ph*.
tips: Never pronounce ভ as v: ভালো is bhalo.
English z words take j: জু (zoo) is ju.
You may say ফ as f; you'll be understood everywhere.

pronunciation.title: Stress on the first syllable and even rhythm
pronunciation.body:
Bengali puts a light **stress on the first syllable** of a word, and in a phrase, on the first word of a group. Unlike English, stress is weak and does not reduce other vowels: every vowel keeps its full quality. Don't swallow the second syllable of বাংলাদেশ: it's *BAṅ-la-desh*, each syllable clear.

Because stress is fixed, English loanwords are re-stressed: কম্পিউটার *KÔMpiuṭar*, টেলিফোন *ṬEliphon*. Speaking with an even, syllable-timed rhythm and a slight emphasis at the start of each phrase will make you sound much more natural.
tips: Tap the table once per syllable; make them all roughly equal length.
Put a gentle emphasis on the first syllable only.
Don't reduce vowels to 'uh' as English does.

pronunciation.title: Intonation: questions and the little word কি
pronunciation.body:
Yes/no questions in Bengali are often made by adding **কি** *ki* after the subject (or just by intonation), with **no change in word order**: তুমি কি বাংলা বলো? *tumi ki baṅla bôlo?* 'Do you speak Bengali?'

The intonation of a yes/no question **rises and then falls sharply at the very end**, on the last syllable: *baṅla bô-LO↗↘?*. This rise-fall sounds unusual to English ears; an English-style final rise can sound uncertain. Question-word questions (কী, কোথায়, কেন…) use a falling tone, like statements. Note the spelling: **কি** is the yes/no particle, **কী** is 'what'; both sound *ki*.

Emphatic particles also shape intonation: **তো** *to* ('after all, right?'), **না** *na* at the end ('…, isn't it?'), and **-ই** *-i* (emphasis 'only, exactly').
tips: For yes/no questions: let the pitch rise and then fall sharply at the very end.
Question words (কী, কোথায়) don't need a rise.
Tag questions end in ..., না? with a rising na.

numbers.note: Also বিশ (bish), the usual word in Bangladesh
